claims.text: The FeNiCrCoCu coating is initially a single-crystal FCC phase on a single-crystal Cu matrix.
The coating initially has a low dislocation density.
Stable chemical short-range order exists in the initial FeNiCrCoCu coating.
At 300–600 K, deformation is dominated by partial-dislocation nucleation and stacking-fault formation.
Interactions among moving dislocations can form Lomer-Cottrell locks.
Stacking-fault networks restrict twin-boundary motion and provide additional work hardening.
Accumulation of dislocations and stacking faults can produce an HCP martensitic transformation.
Above 900 K, thermal activation rapidly annihilates Lomer-Cottrell locks and stacking-fault networks.
Above 900 K, mobile dislocations leave the indentation zone faster than new dislocations are nucleated, causing dislocation starvation.
Increasing lattice disorder and breakdown of chemical short-range order trigger localized amorphization above 900 K.
The sequence of defect annihilation, dislocation starvation, and amorphization changes deformation from FCC work hardening to disorder-dominated softening.
Loss of work-hardening capacity and formation of amorphous regions cause a sharp reduction in hardness.
Localized amorphization increases adhesion, leading to adhesive wear, material transfer, and a spike in friction coefficient.
The HCP atom fraction first rises and then collapses when amorphization becomes dominant.
Total dislocation line length decreases sharply above 900 K because of dislocation annihilation.
Pure disorder-driven thermal softening without amorphization would leave the HCP fraction stable or increasing while dislocation density decreases.
Mechanical annealing would decrease dislocation line length without a corresponding increase in amorphous fraction.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to polycrystalline or multiphase HEAs because grain boundaries provide alternative dislocation sources.
